usage: I feel bad / I'm in a bad mood
나쁘다 = bad; describes the mood, not a person
a change of mood / refreshing break
전환 轉換 = switching; 기분 전환 하다 = lift your spirits
don't make me feel bad / don't offend me
examples: 오늘은 기분이 정말 좋아요.
Today I feel really good.
Simple: 기분이 + adjective is the core frame.
날씨가 흐려서 기분이 안 좋아요.
The weather is gloomy so I'm feeling down.
Everyday: -아서 gives the cause; 안 좋다 softer than 나쁘다.
그 말을 듣고 기분이 좀 상했어요.
I felt a bit hurt after hearing that.
Real situation: 기분이 상하다 = get one's feelings hurt, common after a remark.
nuance: 기분(氣分, literally 'energy-portion') is your momentary emotional weather — how you feel right now — and it rises and falls with events, weather, sleep, or someone's words. Contrast it with 감정 (emotion as a deeper, named state like anger or love) and especially with 행복 (happiness as a lasting condition): 기분이 좋다 is a passing 'I feel good today,' while 행복하다 is 'I am happy with my life.' It is everyday, neutral register and fine with anyone. The big English-speaker trap is the particle: 기분 is the subject of how-you-feel, so it always takes 이 — say 기분이 좋아요, never the object-marked 기분을 좋아요. A second trap is direction: 기분이 좋다 describes YOUR state, so don't use it to call a thing nice; for that use 좋다 alone (이 영화 좋아요).

mistakes: Saying 기분을 좋아요. Wrong particle — 기분 is the thing that is good, i.e. the subject, so it must be 기분이 좋아요.
Translating 'I'm in a good mood' as 행복해요. 행복하다 is lasting life-happiness; for a passing mood say 기분이 좋아요.
Using 느낌 for your inner mood (그 영화 느낌이 좋아요 = the film's vibe). 느낌 is the impression a thing gives off; your own mood is 기분.

usage: 생각하다 = to think; takes 을 as an object
it comes to mind / I remember
나다 = arise; the thought surfaces by itself, so 이
에는 frames 'as for my thought'; set opener
examples: 좋은 생각이 났어요.
A good idea came to me.
Simple: 생각이 나다 — the idea pops up, so subject 이.
저는 가족 생각을 자주 해요.
I often think about my family.
Everyday: 가족 생각을 하다 = to think of family; object 을.
다시 생각해 보니까 제가 틀렸어요.
Thinking it over again, I was wrong.
Real situation: 생각해 보다 = think it through / reconsider.
nuance: 생각 is a pure native-Korean word covering the whole range of English 'thought,' 'idea,' and 'opinion,' so it is wonderfully flexible: 좋은 생각 = a good idea, 제 생각 = my opinion, 생각하다 = to think. The key is how it pairs with verbs. With 하다 (생각을 하다 / 생각하다) it is deliberate, active thinking that YOU do, so the thought is the object → 을. With 나다 (생각이 나다) the thought arises on its own — it surfaces or you suddenly remember — so it is the subject → 이. Contrast 생각하다 with 기억하다: 생각나다 is the thought spontaneously popping up ('it came to me'), while 기억하다 is the willed act of recalling stored memory. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing these two patterns and saying 생각이 해요; if the verb is 하다, you must mark 생각을.

Using 생각하다 where 'remember' is meant. 어제 일이 생각나요 = it comes to mind; deliberate recall of facts is 기억하다.

usage: I like it / it suits me
에 들다 = enters my heart; fixed idiom
I open my heart / open up
편하다 = comfortable; inner peace, not the body
examples: 그 사람은 마음이 따뜻해요.
That person has a warm heart.
Simple: 마음이 + adjective describes someone's inner nature.
이 선물이 정말 마음에 들어요.
I really like this gift.
Everyday: 마음에 들다 is THE verb for liking things/people you encounter.
미안한 마음에 먼저 연락했어요.
Feeling sorry, I reached out first.
Real situation: 마음에 = 'out of (a feeling),' a common motive marker.
nuance: 마음 is the native word for the heart-mind: the seat of feelings, will, intentions, and disposition — never the physical organ (that is 심장 心臟, the pump). Contrast it with 생각 (thought/idea, the cognitive content) and with 기분 (a passing mood): 마음 is the deeper, more stable inner self where kindness, sincerity, and intentions live. It anchors many high-frequency idioms: 마음에 들다 (to like / be pleased by something you meet), 마음을 먹다 (to make up one's mind), 마음이 아프다 (to be heartsick). The classic English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: using 마음 for the body-heart (say 심장이 빨리 뛰어요 for a racing heart), and translating 'I like it' as 좋아해요 when you mean a settled approval of something in front of you — Koreans naturally reach for 마음에 들어요 there, where 좋아하다 is a broader 'I like/am fond of.'

usage: I dream / I have a dream (asleep)
꿈을 꾸다 = the only natural verb for dreaming
I make a dream come true
이루다 = fulfill; 이뤄요 is the 요-form
꿈에 나오다 = show up in a dream
examples: 어젯밤에 좋은 꿈을 꿨어요.
Last night I had a good dream.
Simple: 꿈을 꾸다 — note the same-root verb, like 'dream a dream.'
저는 의사가 되는 게 꿈이에요.
My dream is to become a doctor.
Everyday: 꿈 as a life goal, framed with -는 게 ... 이에요.
포기하지 말고 꿈을 꼭 이루세요.
Don't give up — be sure to make your dream come true.
Real situation: 꿈을 이루다 = achieve a dream, encouraging tone.
nuance: 꿈 is a single native word that carries both English senses at once — the images you see while asleep AND a cherished hope or life goal — so 꿈이 있어요 can mean 'I had a dream (last night)' or 'I have a dream (ambition),' resolved by context. Its signature feature is the cognate-object verb 꿈을 꾸다, literally 'to dream a dream,' which is the ONLY natural way to say you dreamt; for goals the partner verb is 꿈을 이루다 (to fulfill a dream). Contrast 꿈 (an inner, often emotional aspiration) with 목표 目標 (a concrete, measurable target you set and tick off) and 희망 希望 (hope as a hopeful attitude). The big English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the all-purpose 하다 and saying 꿈을 해요 — that is meaningless; dreaming must be 꿈을 꾸다. A second trap: don't use 보다 ('see') for dreams as in some languages; Korean dreams are 'dreamt' (꾸다), and a figure 'comes out' in them (꿈에 나오다).

Saying 꿈을 봤어요 ('I saw a dream'). Korean dreams are dreamt, not seen — use 꿈을 꿨어요.

usage: 사랑하다, the verb; object marker often dropped
에 빠지다 = fall into; fixed idiom
사랑을 받다 = be loved, very common
examples: 저는 가족을 많이 사랑해요.
I love my family a lot.
Simple: 사랑하다 takes the loved one as object (가족을).
그 사람과 사랑에 빠졌어요.
I fell in love with that person.
Everyday: 와/과 ... 사랑에 빠지다 = fall in love WITH someone.
부모님께 많은 사랑을 받고 자랐어요.
I grew up receiving lots of love from my parents.
Real situation: 사랑을 받다 + 자라다 = a natural 'raised with love' frame.
nuance: 사랑 is the native word for love across the full range — romantic, familial, and affection for friends or even things — and with 하다 it becomes 사랑하다, the verb whose object is the beloved (가족을 사랑해요). Note the register: 사랑해(요) is a weighty, sincere declaration. Koreans say it warmly to family and partners, but to acquaintances or in casual liking they prefer the lighter 좋아하다 ('I like you / I'm fond of you') — confessing 좋아해요 is in fact the standard first step, with 사랑해요 saved for deeper commitment. Two key idioms: 사랑에 빠지다 (to fall in love, lit. 'fall into love') and 사랑을 받다 (to be loved). The English-speaker pitfall is the all-purpose-하다 error 사랑이 해요 (the loved one is the object → 사랑을 / 사랑해요), and over-using 'I love' — English 'I love pizza' should be 피자를 좋아해요, since 사랑하다 for food sounds melodramatic.

Using 사랑하다 for casual liking of things. 'I love coffee' = 커피를 좋아해요, not 커피를 사랑해요 (sounds exaggerated).

usage: I have a lot of worries
걱정이 되다 = worry arises on its own
examples: 저는 요즘 걱정이 많아요.
These days I have a lot of worries.
Simple: 걱정이 많다 — worries exist (subject 이).
엄마가 제 건강을 걱정해요.
My mom worries about my health.
Everyday: 걱정하다 takes what's worried about as object (건강을).
걱정하지 마세요. 다 잘될 거예요.
Don't worry. Everything will be fine.
Real situation: 걱정하지 마세요 + reassurance, very natural comfort.
nuance: 걱정 is care or anxiety about something uncertain — the knot in your stomach over a result, a person's health, or money. It splits across two verbs: active 걱정하다 ('to worry about X,' X = object → 건강을 걱정해요) and spontaneous 걱정이 되다 ('X worries me / I become worried,' the worry arises → subject 이). Contrast 걱정 with 고민 (a problem you are mulling over, more like deliberation/a dilemma you turn in your mind) and with 불안 不安 (free-floating anxiety/unease without a clear object): you 걱정 about a specific thing, you 고민 over a decision, you feel 불안 as a mood. The most useful chunk is 걱정하지 마세요/걱정 마 — the go-to way to comfort someone. The English-speaker pitfall is the 하다 particle error 걱정이 해요 (use 걱정을 해요), and saying 걱정에 대해 생각해요 when you simply mean 걱정해요.

Forgetting the object marker: '엄마가 제 건강 걱정해요' is casual-OK, but the full form is 건강을 걱정해요 — the thing worried about takes 을.

usage: 생기다 = come into being; subject 이
examples: 여기 작은 문제가 하나 있어요.
There's one small problem here.
Simple: 문제가 있다 — a problem exists (subject 이).
수학 문제를 다 풀었어요.
I solved all the math problems.
Everyday: 문제를 풀다 also covers test questions; object 를.
그건 전혀 문제가 안 돼요.
That's not a problem at all.
Real situation: 문제가 되다 / 안 되다 = (not) become an issue.
nuance: 문제(問題, 'ask + topic') has two everyday senses English keeps apart: a trouble or difficulty ('we have a problem') AND a question on a test or exercise ('problem 3'). Crucially, both are solved with the same verb 풀다 (literally 'to untie/loosen') — 문제를 풀다 works for a math item and for a real-life difficulty alike, where English would switch to 'answer' vs 'solve.' Other key partners: 문제가 생기다 (a problem arises), 문제가 되다 (to become an issue), and the handy one-word 문제없어요 ('no problem'). Contrast 문제 with 질문 (a question you ASK someone to get information) — a test 문제 is a problem to solve, but raising your hand to ask is 질문하다, not 문제하다. The English-speaker pitfall is the subject/object split: existence and arising take 이 (문제가 있다/생기다), but solving takes 를 (문제를 풀다) — learners often say 문제가 풀어요.

examples: 늦은 이유가 있어요.
There's a reason I'm late.
Simple: 이유가 있다 — a reason exists (subject 이).
저에게 그 이유를 말해 주세요.
Please tell me the reason.
Everyday: 이유를 말하다 — state the reason; object 를.
특별한 이유 없이 그냥 왔어요.
I just came for no particular reason.
Real situation: 이유 없이 = 'for no reason,' with 그냥 ('just').
nuance: 이유(理由, 'principle + cause') is the reason or grounds behind something — the 'why.' Distinguish it from two neighbors: 원인 原因 is the objective CAUSE in a cause-and-effect chain (the cause of a fire, an illness — 화재의 원인), more clinical and used for events, whereas 이유 is the reason/justification a person gives for an action or feeling (늦은 이유). 까닭 is a native near-synonym of 이유 but sounds more literary. Useful frames: 이유가 있다 (there's a reason), 무슨 이유로 (for what reason), and the adverbial 이유 없이 (for no reason). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle split again — stating a reason is transitive (이유를 말하다), so 이유가 말해요 is wrong; and don't translate 'the reason why' with a double marker — Korean just modifies the noun: 제가 온 이유 ('the reason I came'), no 왜 needed inside.

examples: 더 쉬운 방법이 있어요.
There's an easier way.
Simple: 방법이 있다 — a way exists (subject 이).
저는 새로운 방법을 찾고 있어요.
I'm looking for a new method.
Everyday: 방법을 찾다 — seek a method; object 을.
이 방법으로 하면 훨씬 빨라요.
If you do it this way, it's much faster.
Real situation: 방법으로 하다 = do it by/in this way; instrumental 으로.
nuance: 방법(方法, 'direction + rule/law') is the method, means, or how-to of doing something — the practical 'way' to reach a result. Its hallmark particle is 으로 ('by means of'): 이 방법으로 하다 = 'do it this way,' the natural answer to 'how?' Contrast 방법 with 방식 方式, which is a style or manner/mode of doing (한국 방식 = the Korean way of doing things, a habitual pattern), whereas 방법 is a concrete procedure that solves a task; and with 길, which literally means 'road/path' but extends to a metaphorical 'way out' (해결할 길이 없다). Common verbs: 방법을 찾다 (find a way), 방법을 알다/모르다 (know/not know how). The English-speaker pitfall is the existence-vs-action particle (방법이 있다 but 방법을 찾다 — learners say 방법이 찾아요), and reaching for 길 ('way/road') where 방법 is meant: '한국어를 배우는 좋은 방법' not '좋은 길.'

structuredNuance.t: 방법 is the method, means, or how-to of doing something — the practical 'way' to reach a result. Its hallmark particle is 으로 ('by means of'): 이 방법으로 하다 = 'do it this way,' the natural answer to 'how?' Common verbs: 방법을 찾다 (find a way), 방법을 알다/모르다 (know/not know how).

Contrast 방법 with 방식 方式, which is a style or manner/mode of doing (한국 방식 = the Korean way of doing things, a habitual pattern), whereas 방법 is a concrete procedure that solves a task; and with 길, which literally means 'road/path' but extends to a metaphorical 'way out' (해결할 길이 없다).
方法, 'direction + rule/law.'
The pitfall is the existence-vs-action particle (방법이 있다 but 방법을 찾다 — learners say 방법이 찾아요), and reaching for 길 ('way/road') where 방법 is meant: '한국어를 배우는 좋은 방법' not '좋은 길.'

mistakes: Saying 방법이 찾아요. Finding a way is transitive — the way is the object → 방법을 찾아요.
Using 길 for a how-to. '학습 방법' (study method), not '학습 길'; 길 stays for roads or a metaphorical 'way out.'
Marking the means with 로 ... 을: it's 이 방법으로 하다 (instrumental 으로), not 이 방법을 해요.

usage: 세우다 = set up/erect; THE verb for plans
examples: 저는 여행 계획을 세우고 있어요.
I'm making a travel plan.
Simple: 계획을 세우다 — the fixed verb, lit. 'erect a plan.'
오늘 저녁에 특별한 계획이 있어요?
Do you have special plans this evening?
Everyday: 계획이 있다 — a plan exists (subject 이).
모든 게 계획대로 잘 진행됐어요.
Everything went well, just as planned.
Real situation: 계획대로 = 'as planned,' a very natural phrase.
nuance: 계획(計劃, 'count/reckon + plan') is a worked-out plan or scheme for the future. Its single most important quirk is the verb: Koreans BUILD a plan with 세우다 (literally 'to erect/stand up') — 계획을 세우다 — not 만들다 ('make') as the English calque suggests. Other partners: 계획이 있다 (have a plan) and the smooth adverb 계획대로 ('as planned'). Distinguish 계획 from 예정 豫定, which is a SCHEDULED arrangement that is already set ('내일 출발할 예정이에요' = I'm scheduled/due to leave tomorrow), and from 약속, a personal commitment/appointment with someone — 계획 is your own roadmap, 예정 is a fixed scheduling, 약속 involves another party. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly 계획을 만들다 (use 세우다), and translating 'plan to do' with 계획 as a verb — Korean uses -(으)려고 하다 or -(으)ㄹ 계획이다: 여행할 계획이에요 ('I plan to travel'), not 여행을 계획해요 in casual speech.

usage: 어기다 = break/violate; the opposite of 지키다
examples: 우리 내일 만나기로 약속했어요.
We promised to meet tomorrow.
Simple: -기로 약속하다 = promise to do something.
오늘 저녁에 친구하고 약속이 있어요.
I have plans with a friend tonight.
Everyday: 약속이 있다 — note this means an appointment, not a vow.
약속을 꼭 지킬게요. 걱정 마세요.
I'll definitely keep my promise. Don't worry.
Real situation: 약속을 지키다 + -ㄹ게요 commitment, reassuring tone.
nuance: 약속(約束, literally 'bind + tie' — a tying-together of words) carries two English senses Koreans treat as one: a PROMISE (a verbal commitment) and an APPOINTMENT/plans to meet someone. So 약속이 있어요 almost always means 'I have plans (to meet a person),' which surprises English speakers expecting 'I have a promise.' The signature collocations come as an opposed pair: 약속을 지키다 (keep a promise, lit. 'protect') vs 약속을 어기다 (break it, lit. 'violate'). Contrast 약속 with 예약 豫約 (a RESERVATION/booking for a restaurant, hotel, or hospital — 식당 예약), which is institutional, and with 계획 (your own plan, no other party). The English-speaker pitfalls: the 하다 particle slip 약속이 해요 (use 약속을 해요); using 약속 for a restaurant booking (that is 예약); and saying 약속을 깨다 — while understood, the idiomatic 'break a promise' is 약속을 어기다, whereas 깨다 ('shatter') fits cancelling an appointment (약속을 깨다 = bail on plans).

usage: I have a lot of experience
쌓다 = pile up; the idiomatic verb
examples: 저는 일한 경험이 많아요.
I have a lot of work experience.
Simple: 경험이 많다 — experience exists in quantity (subject 이).
외국에서 산 경험을 했어요.
I had the experience of living abroad.
Everyday: 경험을 하다 — go through something; object 을.
인턴을 하면서 경험을 많이 쌓았어요.
I built up a lot of experience while interning.
Real situation: 경험을 쌓다 = accumulate experience, common on résumés.
nuance: 경험(經驗, 'pass through + test/prove') is experience in both English senses: the accumulated know-how you gain over time AND a single event you live through ('a good experience'). The standout collocation is 경험을 쌓다 ('to pile up experience'), the natural way to say you build/gain experience — more idiomatic than 경험을 얻다. Contrast 경험 with 경력 經歷, which is your formal CAREER record / work history as listed on a résumé (경력 3년 = 3 years' career), whereas 경험 is broader lived experience including non-work events; and with 추억, which is a fond MEMORY you look back on emotionally, not the experience itself. Verbs: active 경험하다/경험을 하다 (object → 을) vs stative 경험이 있다/많다 (subject → 이). The English-speaker pitfall is the 하다 particle error 경험이 해요 (use 경험을 해요), and mixing up 경험 with 경력 — when an interviewer asks about your 경력, they want your job history, not a nice trip you took.
